tagline: A lakeside road connects mining history with a relocated town.
intro: The Trinity Heritage Scenic Byway runs north from Weaverville toward Interstate 5 near Weed, following a corridor of lake shore and mountains. Its SR 3 section follows Trinity Lake and crosses the Scott Mountains. A National Forest Scenic Byway, it introduces the area’s history, peoples and resource management through a Forest Service driving tour with 17 stops.

The highway’s identity came together in stages. In 1959, the state extended Route 82 south from Etna to Route 20 near Weaverville, filling a gap in the highway system. Between those changes, Trinity River Dam created the lake in 1961, submerging the original Trinity Center. Several buildings were moved to the town’s present location. The Peanut-to-Montague roadway received the SR 3 number in 1964. The byway uses only part of that longer highway: the section from Weaverville to Gazelle Callahan Road.

Start in Weaverville, where worship continues at the Joss House temple. Northward, the lake corridor leads past Covington Mill to Trinity Center, whose original stage-stop site lies beneath the reservoir. Beyond Trinity Center and Coffee Creek, SR 3 parallels the Trinity River before crossing the Scott Mountains. The byway leaves SR 3 at Gazelle Callahan Road and finishes at Interstate 5 north of Weed.

moments.title: Weaverville Joss House
moments.text: In 1989, a box left at the visitor center returned a Chinese Guardian Lion stolen from the temple in 1934. Chinese goldminers built the first temple in 1853; the present building replaced fire-destroyed predecessors in 1874. After that theft, local resident Moon Lim Lee became trustee and campaigned for state protection. The site became a state historic site in 1956. California commissioned a new pair of guardian figures from traditional craftsmen in China for display in the temple. Worship continues at this Taoist temple, and a lion dance celebrates Chinese New Year.

moments.title: Bowerman Barn
moments.text: Jacob Bowerman built this barn by hand in 1878, using whipsawn pine and board-and-batten siding. His ranch supplied beef and dairy products to wholesalers and businesses in Minersville. The ranch also included a house, milk house and wagon shed, all later lost to fire. After Bowerman died in 1917, the barn served sheep farming and storage until the Forest Service bought the property in 1974. The historic barn is on Guy Covington Drive southwest of Trinity Center. The barn entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1981, seven years after the federal purchase.

moments.title: Trinity Center
moments.text: The original Trinity Center lies beneath the lake. Established in 1851 as a stage stop for travelers continuing north, it was also a gold-mining town. The lake formed after construction of Trinity River Dam in 1961. A handful of buildings moved to the present town, including the I.O.O.F. building and several residences.
